newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SOUTH AFRICA'S ERWIN SEES PRIVATE INVESTMENT BOOM.
newsitem.headline: SOUTH AFRICA'S ERWIN SEES PRIVATE INVESTMENT BOOM.

text.p: South Africa's long term internal investment agenda looks better halfway through the first term of democratic government than it has looked in 20 years, Trade and Industry Minister Alec Erwin said on Monday.

Erwin, in South Africa between visits to Europe this month and to India and Singapore next month, told businessmen in Cape Town that trade with neighbours in the 13-nation Southern African Development Community also was growing at a record pace.
"From the point of view of investment performance and announced investment plans, things are looking very strong," he said at a meeting organised by the Western Cape provincial government.

"The forward planning announcements of investments by South African corporations in the last six months amount to a greater forward planning of invesment than we have seen for nearly 20 years in this economy," he said.

President Nelson Mandela's African National Congress government marked the halfway point earlier this month in its five-year term of office following the country's first democratic elections in April 1994.
Erwin said longer term and macro-economic indicators remained strongly positive despite the devaluation of the rand against the dollar of more than 20 percent since February.
"On every count that you can look at, outside the logic of financial markets, the South African economy remains very sound in its growth path.

"On the real economy side, confidence remains strong, investment is performing very well. What we are working on and will need to take action on is clearly the financial evaluation of the rand," he said.

Erwin pointed to inflation still in single figures, positive private sector investment, growing exports, fiscal discipline in line with targets set in the March budget and rising productivity in relation to labour costs.

He said the positive response to the new government's policies was reflected in an almost embarassing rise in exports to SADC countries, which fear being overwhelmed by the region's economic superpower.
"In every SADC country in the southern African region, our trade surplusses in our favour are growing at above 50 percent per annum," he said.
Though some of these countries were recording economic growth in excess of South Africa's three percent, this was not enough to account for the burgeoning trade suplus.
"It must mean that South African exporters are very rapidly displacing exporters from elsewhere. It looks like they are displacing exporters from the European Union," he said.

Erwin said the growth reflected an economic success for South Africa, but sounded a warning for the medium term about the country's promise that it will share its economic growth with its neighbours in the region.
Erwin said the government also was concerned about sharing growth with smaller enterprises and was reviewing existing legislation to ensure easier access.
"We are looking at a range of business practices that presently either inhibit access to a market or abuse people by misleading them, falsifying information.
"We need an efficient, transparent regime that governs our internal trading relations. That's going to help investment, its going to help trade," he said.
